gist: Labour is considering options to raise funds without increasing income tax, VAT or National Insurance.
Potential measures include higher bank surcharges, gambling taxes, online VAT enforcement and welfare cuts.
The government faces shrinking fiscal headroom alongside pressures from living costs and defence spending.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government faces a shrinking fiscal buffer, which economists estimate may have fallen from £24bn to £11bn. With manifesto pledges ruling out increases to income tax, VAT, or National Insurance, options to raise revenue include raising the corporation tax surcharge on banks and doubling the tax on electronic gaming machines. Another proposal would make online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu responsible for collecting VAT owed by platform sellers. Reducing welfare spending is also being considered.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Chancellor John Healey needs funds to maintain fiscal rules, support defence spending and assist with the cost of living. The proposed tax measures could raise around £3.5bn annually, though critics highlight potential downsides. Gambling taxes could worsen odds for users, and online sellers might raise consumer prices. Restricting health and disability benefits could push recipients into poverty, while experts caution that required back-to-work support might offset immediate savings.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Chancellor is expected to present the Budget on Wednesday. Any welfare reforms may face political hurdles, following previous backbench revolts over proposed benefit reductions.

sections.text: Chancellor John Healey delivered a budget featuring ninety-eight different spending measures, including council tax reductions and a future defence spending target. The speech lacked jokes and generated a sombre mood.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The budget was intended to provide breathing space and public finance urgency, yet it avoided major decisions, leaving growth low and living standards falling.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Sophie Price was denied hospital meals while staying with her critically ill daughter Florence because she was formula feeding instead of breastfeeding. The family spent over one thousand pounds on canteen and takeaway food during a three-week hospital stay.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The health board policy provides meals to breastfeeding mums to support nutrition, while paediatric ward policy does not classify mothers as patients unless breastfeeding. Critics call this policy outdated and discriminatory against formula-feeding mothers.

gist: NHS Western Isles prescribes weight loss drugs at triple the rate of others.
A new report highlights substantial geographic variation in access to GLP-1 medications across Scotland.
Small island populations and pilot schemes may affect the recorded prescribing rates.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A report compared access to new medicines across Scottish health boards from September 2020 to August 2025. It found NHS Western Isles prescribed GLP-1 medications at the highest rate, triple that of other health boards, while NHS Shetland had the lowest rate.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The analysis shows substantial geographic variation in patient access to medicines judged safe and value for money, which authors say cannot be fully explained by differences in patient need.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The report makes seven recommendations, including better planning, co-operation, and increased transparency by health boards regarding local decisions on medicine use.
